{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_3","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"sed -n '1,260p' /app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md\"","aggregated_output":"# Conversion Notes: MAP Dataset to Decoder Format\n\n## Source Data\n- **Dataset**: \"Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement\" (MAP dataset)\n- **Format**: 174 NWB files (Neurodata Without Borders)\n- **Task**: Auditory delayed response task with 3kHz/12kHz tones, 1.2s delay, Go cue, lick left/right response\n\n## Processing Parameters\n- **Temporal alignment**: Go cue onset (t=0)\n- **Time window**: -2.5s to +1.5s (4s total)\n- **Bin size**: 50ms non-overlapping bins -> 80 time bins\n- **Neural data**: Spike counts per bin, converted to firing rates (spikes/s)\n\n## Filtering Criteria\n\n### Session Filtering\n- Behavioral performance > 65% correct on control (non-photostimulation) trials\n- At least 50 correct lick-left AND 50 correct lick-right control trials\n- Performance computed on ALL session trials (not just recorded subset)\n- **Result**: 144 of 174 sessions passed (30 skipped: 21 low performance, 6 insufficient correct trials per side, 1 no good units, 2 other)\n\n### Unit Filtering\n- Only units with `classification == 'good'` (from quality control classifiers)\n- Units must have a valid CCF annotation (`anno_name`) that maps to one of 14 brain regions\n- **Result**: 57,935 good units across 144 sessions (paper reports 69,943 across 173 sessions; difference due to session filtering and NWB file count)\n\n### Trial Filtering\n- Exclude `auto_water` and `free_water` trials\n- Keep all other trials including early lick and no-response (ignore) trials\n- Only include trials covered by neural recordings (via `obs_intervals`)\n\n## Key Decisions\n\n### Tone Onset Timing\nTone onset is consistently 1.85s before Go cue across all sessions. This was determined by comparing `sample_start_times` to `go_start_times` in the NWB trial tables. The value matches the task structure: sample epoch (3 tones x 150ms + 2 gaps x 100ms = 650ms) + delay epoch (1200ms) = 1850ms.\n\n### obs_intervals Alignment\nEach unit's `obs_intervals` defines which trials have valid neural coverage. The first obs_interval does NOT always correspond to trial 0 — some sessions start recording mid-session. We match by finding the trial whose `start_time` is closest to the first `obs_interval` start time, then assign sequential trial indices from there.\n\n### Brain Region Mapping\nCCF (Allen Brain Atlas Common Coordinate Framework) annotations are mapped to 14 broad regions matching the original paper's analysis:\n- **ALM**: Secondary motor area\n- **OtherCortex**: Primary motor, somatosensory, visual, auditory, cingulate, etc.\n- **Orbital**: Orbital areas, Frontal pole\n- **Striatum**: Caudoputamen, nucleus accumbens\n- **Pallidum**: Globus pallidus, septal nuclei, bed nuclei, substantia innominata\n- **Thalamus**: All thalamic nuclei including paracentral, parafascicular, anterodorsal, anteromedial, rhomboid, perireunensis, habenula, geniculate\n- **Hypothalamus**: Hypothalamic areas, zona incerta, subthalamic nucleus\n- **Hippocampus**: CA fields, dentate gyrus, subiculum, entorhinal\n- **Olfactory**: Olfactory areas, piriform, taenia tecta\n- **CorticalSubplate**: Amygdala, claustrum, endopiriform\n- **Midbrain**: Superior/inferior colliculus, substantia nigra, VTA, PAG\n- **Pons**: Pontine nuclei, parabrachial, locus ceruleus\n- **Medulla**: Reticular nuclei, trigeminal, vestibular, facial motor\n- **Cerebellum**: Lobules, deep cerebellar nuclei\n\nAn initial run identified 835 thalamic units whose CCF names lacked the word \"thalamus\" (e.g., \"Paracentral nucleus\", \"Parafascicular nucleus\"). These were added as explicit matches.\n\n### Decoder Inputs\n1. **time_from_tone_onset** (continuous): Time of each bin center relative to tone onset. Range: [-0.6, 3.3]s. Same for all trials (deterministic from bin structure).\n2. **photostimulation** (binary): 1 if photostimulation trial, 0 otherwise. From NWB `photo_stim_type` column.\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n1. **choice** (binary): 0=left, 1=right. From NWB `trial_instruction` column.\n2. **outcome** (3 classes): 0=ignore (no response), 1=miss (wrong lick), 2=hit (correct). Derived from `outcome` and `early_lick` columns.\n3. **early_lick** (binary): 0=no early lick, 1=early lick. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n    20→\\n    21→To analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\n    22→time window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n    23→\\n    24→Spike sorting and quality control\\n    25→\\n    26→We developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n    27→\\n    28→The details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. This corresponds to 25.9 % of clusters reported by Kilosort2. \\n    29→\\n\\n[metadata] {\\\"type\\\": \\\"text\\\", \\\"file\\\": {\\\"filePath\\\": \\\"/app/methods.txt\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"Behavior and video tracking\\\\n\\\\nMice performed an auditory delayed response task 21 (Figure 1A). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\\\n\\\\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\\\n\\\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\\\n\\\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\\\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\\\n\\\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\\\n\\\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\\\n\\\\nPhotoinhibition\\\\n\\\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\\\n\\\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\\\n\\\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\\\n\\\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\\\n\\\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\n\\nPhotoinhibition\\n\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\n\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\n     5→response trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n     8→\\n     9→Multi-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n    10→\\n    11→We designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n    14→\\n    15→Probes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n    27→\\n    28→The details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\\\n\\\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\\\n\\\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\\\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\\\n\\\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\\\n\\\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\\\n\\\\nPhotoinhibition\\\\n\\\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\\\n\\\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\\\n\\\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\\\n\\\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\\\n\\\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\n     4→quency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\n     5→response trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\n     6→\\n     7→Two CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). VideoAnalysisUtils.preprocessing_utils as preprocessing_utils\\n    19→\\n    20→\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    21→Important notes on reading MATLAB files using Python:\\n    22→When we read an Nx1 MATLAB cell into a length-N Python list/array/anything iterable (and potentially do something before storing it into an iterable, e.g. if the cell contains indices, we might need to subtract 1 from each element since MATLAB counts from 1 and Python counts from 0), pay attention to the following three cases:\\n    23→1. Empty 0x1 cell. Need to manually define what it becomes in Python.\\n    24→2. 1x1 cell. Will be directly read as non-iterables such as str, int, float, etc. Need to manually convert it to an iterable with length 1.\\n    25→3. Nx1 cell (N >= 2). Usually it's fine to read and directly store it in Python.\\n    26→\\n    27→Comment: in case 2, when using isinstance(data, data_type), if data could be a number, consider the possibility of data being either float or int, i.e. use\\n    28→    if isinstance(data, float) or isinstance(data, int):\\n    29→        do something\\n    30→\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    31→\\n    32→plt.rcParams['pdf.fonttype'] = 42\\n    33→plt.rcParams['ps.fonttype'] = 42\\n    34→\\n    35→\\n    36→def sliding_histogram(spikeTimes, begin_time, end_time, bin_width, stride, rate=True):\\n    37→    '''\\n    38→    Calculates the number of spikes for each unit in each sliding bin of width bin_width, strided by stride.\\n    39→    begin_time and end_time are treated as the lower- and upper- bounds for bin centers.\\n    40→    if rate=True, calculate firing rates instead of bin spikes.\\n    41→    '''\\n    42→    bin_begin_time = begin_time\\n    43→    bin_end_time = end_time\\n    44→    # This is to deal with cases where for e.g. (bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride is actually 43 but evaluates to 42.999999... due to numerical errors in floating-point arithmetic.\\n    45→    if np.allclose((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride, math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1):\\n    46→        n_bins =  math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+2\\n    47→    else:\\n    48→        n_bins = math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1\\n    49→    binCenters = bin_begin_time + np.arange(n_bins)*stride\\n    50→\\n    51→    binIntervals = np.vstack((binCenters-bin_width/2, binCenters+bin_width/2)).T\\n    52→\\n    53→    # Count number of spikes for each sliding bin\\n    54→    binSpikes = np.asarray([[[np.sum(np.all([trial>=binInt[0], trial<binInt[1]], axis=0)) for binInt in binIntervals] for trial in unit]\\n    55→        for unit in spikeTimes]).swapaxes(0,-1)\\n    56→\\n    57→    if rate:\\n    58→        return binCenters, binSpikes/float(bin_width) # get firing rates\\n    59→    return binCenters, binSpikes\\n    60→\\n    61→\\n    62→def process_one_sess(data_folder, file_path_list, bw, stride, begin_time=-3.0, end_time=3.5, save_folder=os.path.join(os.pardir, 'data_processed'), qc_mode='classifier'):\\n    63→    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    64→    Process all probe files in one session.\\n    65→\\n    66→    Args:\\n    67→        data_folder (str): the folder containing all data including QC neuron ID files.\\n    68→        file_path_list: list of full file paths of all probes in this session.\\n    69→        bw (float): in sec.\\n    70→        stride (float): in sec.\\n    71→        qc_mode (str): 'classifier' or 'old'.\\n    72→    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    73→    print(qc_mode)\\n    74→    if qc_mode == 'classifier':\\n    75→        qc_folder = os.path.join(data_folder, 'goodunits')\\n    76→        print(qc_folder)\\n    77→    elif qc_mode == 'old':\\n    78→        qc_folder = os.path.join(data_folder, 'DJ_GoodUnitsIdx_14regions_old_qc')\\n    79→    else:\\n    80→        raise ValueError('Wrong qc_mode! HERE\\n   328→            area_dict_exist = pickle.load(f)\\n   329→            fr = area_dict_exist['fr']\\n   330→            spike_times_area = area_dict_exist['spike_times']\\n   331→            bin_centers = area_dict_exist['bin_centers']\\n   332→\\n   333→    # Empty 0x1 cell. Need to manually define what it becomes in Python.\\n2. 1x1 cell. Will be directly read as non-iterables such as str, int, float, etc. Need to manually convert it to an iterable with length 1.\\n3. Nx1 cell (N >= 2). Usually it's fine to read and directly store it in Python.\\n\\nComment: in case 2, when using isinstance(data, data_type), if data could be a number, consider the possibility of data being either float or int, i.e. use\\n    if isinstance(data, float) or isinstance(data, int):\\n        do something\\n\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n\\nplt.rcParams['pdf.fonttype'] = 42\\nplt.rcParams['ps.fonttype'] = 42\\n\\n\\ndef sliding_histogram(spikeTimes, begin_time, end_time, bin_width, stride, rate=True):\\n    '''\\n    Calculates the number of spikes for each unit in each sliding bin of width bin_width, strided by stride.\\n    begin_time and end_time are treated as the lower- and upper- bounds for bin centers.\\n    if rate=True, calculate firing rates instead of bin spikes.\\n    '''\\n    bin_begin_time = begin_time\\n    bin_end_time = end_time\\n    # This is to deal with cases where for e.g. (bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride is actually 43 but evaluates to 42.999999... due to numerical errors in floating-point arithmetic.\\n    if np.allclose((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride, math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1):\\n        n_bins =  math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+2\\n    else:\\n        n_bins = math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1\\n    binCenters = bin_begin_time + np.arange(n_bins)*stride\\n\\n    binIntervals = np.vstack((binCenters-bin_width/2, binCenters+bin_width/2)).T\\n\\n    # Count number of spikes for each sliding bin\\n    54→    binSpikes = np.asarray([[[np.sum(np.all([trial>=binInt[0], trial<binInt[1]], axis=0)) for binInt in binIntervals] for trial in unit]\\n    55→        for unit in spikeTimes]).swapaxes(0,-1)\\n    56→\\n    57→    if rate:\\n    58→        return binCenters, binSpikes/float(bin_width) # NWBHDF5IO\\nimport warnings\\nwarnings.filterwarnings('ignore')\\n\\n# --- Constants ---\\nBIN_WIDTH = 0.05  # 50 ms bins\\nBEGIN_TIME = -2.5  # seconds relative to go cue\\nEND_TIME = 1.5    # seconds relative to go cue\\nTONE_ONSET_REL = -1.85  # tone onset relative to go cue (sample 0.65s + delay 1.2s)\\nMIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE = 50  # minimum correct trials per side for session inclusion\\nMIN_PERFORMANCE = 0.65  # minimum performance for session inclusion\\n\\n# Time bin edges and centers\\nN_BINS = int(round((END_TIME - BEGIN_TIME) / BIN_WIDTH))  # 80\\nBIN_EDGES = np.linspace(BEGIN_TIME, END_TIME, N_BINS + 1)\\nBIN_CENTERS = (BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_EDGES[1:]) / 2\\n\\n# --- Brain region mapping ---\\n# Map CCF annotation names to the 14 broad regions used in the paper\\n# Based on Allen Brain Atlas CCF ontology and paper methodology\\n\\ndef map_anno_to_region(anno_name):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Map a CCF annotation name to one of 14 broad brain regions.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    if not anno_name or anno_name.strip() == '':\\n        return None\\n\\n    a = anno_name.strip()\\n    al = a.lower()\\n\\n    # ALM: Secondary motor area (= Anterior Lateral Motor cortex)\\n    if 'secondary motor area' in al:\\n        return 'ALM'\\n\\n    # Orbital: Orbital areas and Frontal pole\\n    if 'orbital area' in al or 'frontal pole' in al:\\n        return 'Orbital'\\n\\n    # Striatum\\n    if al in ('caudoputamen', 'striatum', 'fundus of striatum', 'nucleus accumbens'):\\n        return 'Striatum'\\n\\n    # Pallidum (including septal nuclei, bed nuclei, substantia innominata per Allen CCF)\\n    if ('globus pallidus' in al or al == 'pallidum' or\\n        'septal nucleus' in al or 'septofimbrial' in al or\\n        'triangular nucleus of septum' in al or\\n        'substantia innominata' in al or\\n        'bed nuclei of the stria terminalis' in al):\\n        return 'Pallidum'\\n\\n    # Hypothalamus (including zona incerta, subthalamic, fields of forel)\\n    if ('hypothalamus' in al or 'hypothalamic' in al or\\n        'zona incerta' in al or 'fields of forel' in al or\\n        'subthalamic' in al or 'lateral preoptic' in al or\\n        'tuberomammillary' in al or 'parasubthalamic' in al or\\n        'posterior hypothalamic' in al or 'lateral hypothalamic' in al):\\n        return 'Hypothalamus'\\n\\n    # Thalamus (check AFTER hypothalamus to avoid matching \\\"hypothalamus\\\")\\n    if ('thalamus' in al or 'habenula' in al or\\n        'lateral geniculate' in al or 'medial geniculate' in al or\\n        'suprageniculate' in al):\\n        return 'Thalamus'\\n\\n    # Cerebellum\\n    if ('cerebellum' in al or 'lobule' in al or 'lobules' in al or\\n        'simple lobule' in al or 'copula' in al or 'nodulus' in al or\\n        'uvula' in al or 'pyramus' in al or 'declive' in al or\\n        'paramedian lobule' in al or 'crus ' in al or 'lingula' in al or\\n        'fastigial' in al or 'interposed nucleus' in al or\\n        'infracerebellar' in al or 'dentate nucleus' in al):\\n        return 'Cerebellum'\\n\\n    # Midbrain\\n    if ('midbrain' in al or 'superior colliculus' in al or\\n        'inferior colliculus' in al or 'substantia nigra' in al or\\n        'red nucleus' in al or 'ventral tegmental' in al or\\n        'pretectal' in al or 'pedunculopontine' in al or\\n        'periaqueductal' in al or 'peripeduncular' in al or\\n        'nucleus of the optic tract' in al or 'nucleus sagulum' in al or\\n        'subparafascicular nucleus' in al or 'subparafascicular area' in al or\\n        'accessory optic tract' in al):\\n        return 'Midbrain'\\n\\n    # Pons\\n    if ('pontine' in al or al == 'pons' or 'parabrachial' in al or\\n        'tegmental reticular' in al or 'koelliker' in al or\\n        'locus ceruleus' in al or 'lateral lemniscus' in al or\\n        'brachium of the inferior colliculus' in al):\\n        return 'Pons'\\n\\n    # Medulla\\n    if ('medulla' in al or 'medullary' in al or\\n        'gigantocellular' in al or 'magnocellular' in al or\\n        'parvicellular' in al or 'paragigantocellular' in al or\\n        'intermediate reticular' in al or 'inferior olivary' in al or\\n        'solitary tract' in al or 'vagus' in al or\\n        'vestibular' in al or 'facial motor' in al or\\n        'trigeminal' in al or 'hypoglossal' in al or\\n        'external cuneate' in al or 'lateral reticular nucleus' in al or\\n        'parasolitary' in al or 'parapyramidal' in al or\\n        'nucleus raphe' in al or 'nucleus of roller' in al or\\n        'nucleus x' in al):\\n        return 'Medulla'\\n\\n    # Hippocampus\\n    if ('field ca' in al or 'dentate gyrus' in al or\\n        'subiculum' in al or 'postsubiculum' in al or\\n        'hippocampal' in al or 'entorhinal' in al):\\n        return 'Hippocampus'\\n\\n    # Olfactory\\n    if ('olfactory' in al or 'piriform' in al or 'taenia tecta' in al):\\n        return 'Olfactory'\\n\\n    # Cortical subplate (amygdala, claustrum, endopiriform)\\n    if ('amygdal' in al or 'claustrum' in al or 'endopiriform' in al or\\n        'cortical subplate' in al or 'intercalated' in al):\\n        return 'CorticalSubplate'\\n\\n    # OtherCortex: remaining cortical areas\\n    cortex_keywords = [\\n        'primary motor', 'primary somatosensory', 'primary visual',\\n        'primary auditory', 'supplemental somatosensory',\\n        'gustatory', 'visceral area', 'retrosplenial',\\n        'temporal association', 'ectorhinal', 'perirhinal',\\n        'anterior cingulate', 'prelimbic', 'infralimbic',\\n        'agranular insular', 'dorsal peduncular',\\n        'dorsal auditory', 'ventral auditory',\\n        'posteromedial visual', 'anteromedial visual',\\n        'area, layer', 'area, layer',  # catch remaining cortical layers\\n    ]\\n    for kw in cortex_keywords:\\n        if kw in al:\\n            return 'OtherCortex'\\n\\n    # If contains \\\"layer\\\" it's likely cortex\\n    if 'layer' in al:\\n        return 'OtherCortex'\\n\\n    # Fallback: print warning and return None\\n    print(f\\\"  WARNING: Unmapped annotation: '{anno_name}'\\\")\\n    return None\\n\\n\\ndef compute_firing_rates(spike_times, go_cue_time, begin_time, end_time, bin_edges):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    Compute firing rates for a single unit across trials.\\n\\n    Args:\\n        spike_times: array of spike times (absolute session time)\\n        go_cue_time: absolute time of go cue for this trial\\n        begin_time, end_time: time window relative to go cue\\n        bin_edges: array of bin edges relative to go cue\\n\\n    Returns:\\n        firing_rates: array of shape (n_bins,) - firing rates in Hz\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    # Convert to relative time\\n    rel_spikes = spike_times - go_cue_time\\n    # Keep only spikes within window\\n    mask = (rel_spikes >= begin_time) & (rel_spikes < end_time)\\n    rel_spikes = rel_spikes[mask]\\n    # Bin spikes\\n    counts, _ = np.histogram(rel_spikes, bins=bin_edges)\\n    # Convert to firing rate (Hz)\\n    firing_rates = counts / BIN_WIDTH\\n    return firing_rates\\n\\n\\ndef process_session(nwb_file, verbose=True):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    Process a single NWB file (session) and return formatted data.\\n\\n    Returns:\\n        session_data dict or None if session doesn't meet criteria\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    io = NWBHDF5IO(nwb_file, 'r')\\n    nwb = io.read()\\n\\n    sess_name = os.path.basename(nwb_file)\\n    subject_id = nwb.subject.subject_id\\n    subject_desc = nwb.subject.description  # e.g. 'SC015'\\n\\n    # --- Get trial info ---\\n    trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\\n    n_trials_total = len(trials)\\n\\n    # --- Get go cue times ---\\n    be = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents']\\n    go_start_times = be.time_series['go_start_times'].timestamps[:]\\n    assert len(go_start_times) == n_trials_total, f\\\"go_start_times ({len(go_start_times)}) != n_trials ({n_trials_total})\\\"\\n\\n    # --- Filter trials: exclude auto_water and free_water ---\\n    valid_trial_mask = (trials['auto_water'].values == 0) & (trials['free_water'].values == 0)\\n\\n    # --- Session filtering: compute performance on CONTROL trials ---\\n    # Control trials = no photostim, no auto_water, no free_water, no early lick\\n    control_mask = (valid_trial_mask &\\n                    (trials['early_lick'].values == 'no early') &\\n                    (trials['outcome'].values != 'ignore'))\\n\\n    # Check photostim: N/A means no photostim\\n    photostim_power = trials['photostim_power'].values\\n    no_photostim = np.array([str(p) == 'N/A' or str(p) == 'nan' or (isinstance(p, (int, float)) and p == 0) for p in photostim_power])\\n    control_mask = control_mask & no_photostim\\n\\n    control_trials = trials[control_mask]\\n    n_control = len(control_trials)\\n\\n    if n_control == 0:\\n        if verbose:\\n            print(f\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: no control trials\\\")\\n        io.close()\\n        return None\\n\\n    # Performance = fraction correct among control trials\\n    n_correct = (control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit').sum()\\n    performance = n_correct / n_control\\n\\n    # Count correct left and right\\n    correct_left = ((control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit') &\\n                    (control_trials['trial_instruction'].values == 'left')).sum()\\n    correct_right = ((control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit') &\\n                     (control_trials['trial_instruction'].values == 'right')).sum()\\n\\n    if performance < MIN_PERFORMANCE:\\n        if verbose:\\n            print(f\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: performance {performance:.2%} < {MIN_PERFORMANCE:.0%}\\\")\\n        io.close()\\n        return None\\n\\n    if correct_left < MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE or correct_right < MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE:\\n        if verbose:\\n            print(f\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: correct L={correct_left}, R={correct_right} (need {MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE})\\\")\\n        io.close()\\n        return None\\n\\n    # --- Get valid trial indices ---\\n    valid_indices = np.where(valid_trial_mask)[0]\\n    n_trials = len(valid_indices)\\n\\n    if n_trials < 2:\\n        if verbose:\\n            print(f\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: only {n_trials} valid trials\\\")\\n        io.close()\\n        return None\\n\\n    # --- Get unit info ---\\n    units = nwb.units\\n    n_units_total = len(units)\\n    classification = units['classification'].data[:]\\n    anno_names = units['anno_name'].data[:]\\n\\n    # Filter to good units with valid annotations\\n    good_mask = classification == 'good'\\n    good_indices = np.where(good_mask)[0]\\n\\n    # Map annotations to regions and filter out unmapped units\\n    unit_regions = []\\n    final_unit_indices = []\\n    for ui in good_indices:\\n        region = map_anno_to_region(anno_names[ui])\\n        if region is not None:\\n            unit_regions.append(region)\\n            final_unit_indices.append(ui)\\n\\n    n_good = len(final_unit_indices)\\n    if n_good == 0:\\n        if verbose:\\n            print(f\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: no good units with valid regions\\\")\\n        io.close()\\n        return None\\n\\n    # --- Compute firing rates for each unit and trial ---\\n    neural_data = []  # list of (n_neurons, n_bins) per trial\\n\\n    for trial_idx in valid_indices:\\n        go_time = go_start_times[trial_idx]\\n        trial_fr = np.zeros((n_good, N_BINS), dtype=np.float32)\\n\\n        for i, ui in enumerate(final_unit_indices):\\n            spike_times = units.get_unit_spike_times(ui)\\n            trial_fr[i, :] = compute_firing_rates(\\n                spike_times, go_time, BEGIN_TIME, END_TIME, BIN_EDGES\\n            )\\n\\n        neural_data.append(trial_fr)\\n\\n    # --- Get photostim times ---\\n    photostim_start_ts = be.time_series['photostim_start_times'].timestamps[:]\\n    photostim_stop_ts = be.time_series['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps[:]\\n\\n    # --- Compute inputs and outputs per trial ---\\n    input_data = []  # list of (2, n_bins) per trial\\n    output_data = []  # list of (4,) per trial\\n\\n    # Get tongue tracking data\\n    bt = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries']\\n    tongue_ts = bt.time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\\n    tongue_data_all = tongue_ts.data[:]  # (n_timepoints, 3): x, y, likelihood\\n    tongue_timestamps = tongue_ts.timestamps[:]\\n\\n    # Compute tongue y percentiles over entire session for discretization\\n    # Use all timepoints (entire session) for percentile computation\\n    tongue_y_all = tongue_data_all[:, 1]\\n    tongue_y_p40 = np.percentile(tongue_y_all, 40)\\n    tongue_y_p60 = np.percentile(tongue_y_all, 60)\\n\\n    for trial_idx in valid_indices:\\n        go_time = go_start_times[trial_idx]\\n        trial_info = trials.iloc[trial_idx]\\n\\n        # --- Input 1: Time from tone onset (continuous, time-varying) ---\\n        time_from_tone = BIN_CENTERS - TONE_ONSET_REL  # relative to tone onset\\n\\n        # --- Input 2: Photostimulation on/off (binary, time-varying) ---\\n        photostim_binary = np.zeros(N_BINS, dtype=np.float32)\\n        # Find photostim events overlapping this trial window\\n        trial_start_abs = go_time + BEGIN_TIME\\n        trial_end_abs = go_time + END_TIME\\n        for ps_start, ps_stop in zip(photostim_start_ts, photostim_stop_ts):\\n            if ps_stop > trial_start_abs and ps_start < trial_end_abs:\\n                # Convert to relative time\\n                rel_start = ps_start - go_time\\n                rel_stop = ps_stop - go_time\\n                # Mark bins where photostim is on\\n                for b in range(N_BINS):\\n                    bc = BIN_CENTERS[b]\\n                    if bc >= rel_start and bc < rel_stop:\\n                        photostim_binary[b] = 1.0\\n\\n        input_trial = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim_binary], axis=0).astype(np.float32)\\n        input_data.append(input_trial)\\n\\n        # --- Output 1: Choice (left=0, right=1) ---\\n        instruction = trial_info['trial_instruction']\\n        outcome = trial_info['outcome']\\n        if outcome == 'hit':\\n            choice = 0 if instruction == 'left' else 1\\n        elif outcome == 'miss':\\n            choice = 1 if instruction == 'left' else 0  # chose opposite\\n        else:  # ignore - no lick, use instruction as proxy\\n            choice = 0 if instruction == 'left' else 1\\n\\n        # --- Output 2: Outcome (ignore=0, miss=1, hit=2) ---\\n        outcome_map = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\\n        outcome_val = outcome_map[outcome]\\n\\n        # --- Output 3: Early lick (no=0, yes=1) ---\\n        early_lick_val = 1 if trial_info['early_lick'] == 'early' else 0\\n\\n        # --- Output 4: Tongue y-position (discretized, time-varying) ---\\n        tongue_y_trial = np.zeros(N_BINS, dtype=np.float32)\\n        for b in range(N_BINS):\\n            bc = BIN_CENTERS[b]\\n            t_abs = go_time + bc\\n            # Find closest tongue timestamp\\n            idx = np.searchsorted(tongue_timestamps, t_abs)\\n            if idx >= len(tongue_timestamps):\\n                idx = len(tongue_timestamps) - 1\\n            elif idx > 0:\\n                # Choose the closer of the two neighbors\\n                if abs(tongue_timestamps[idx] - t_abs) > abs(tongue_timestamps[idx-1] - t_abs):\\n                    idx = idx - 1\\n            y_val = tongue_data_all[idx, 1]\\n            # Discretize\\n            if y_val < tongue_y_p40:\\n                tongue_y_trial[b] = 0\\n            elif y_val <= tongue_y_p60:\\n                tongue_y_trial[b] = 1\\n            else:\\n                tongue_y_trial[b] = 2\\n\\n        # Combine outputs: first 3 are per-trial scalars, last is time-varying\\n        # Per-trial values broadcast to all time bins for the time-varying format\\n        output_choice = np.full(N_BINS, choice, dtype=np.float32)\\n        output_outcome = np.full(N_BINS, outcome_val, dtype=np.float32)\\n        output_early = np.full(N_BINS, early_lick_val, dtype=np.float32)\\n\\n        output_trial = np.stack([output_choice, output_outcome, output_early, tongue_y_trial], axis=0).astype(np.float32)\\n        output_data.append(output_trial)\\n\\n    if verbose:\\n        print(f\\\"  OK {sess_name}: {n_good} units, {n_trials} trials, perf={performance:.2%}, \\\"\\n              f\\\"L={correct_left}, R={correct_right}, sub={subject_desc}\\\")\\n\\n    io.close()\\n\\n    return {\\n        'neural': neural_data,\\n        'input': input_data,\\n        'output': output_data,\\n        'unit_regions': unit_regions,\\n        'subject_id': subject_id,\\n        'subject_desc': subject_desc,\\n        'n_good': n_good,\\n        'n_trials': n_trials,\\n        'performance': performance,\\n        'correct_left': correct_left,\\n        'correct_right': correct_right,\\n        'sess_name': sess_name,\\n    }\\n\\n\\ndef convert_all(data_dir='data', output_file='converted_data.pkl', sample_output_file='sample_data.pkl',\\n                max_sessions=None, verbose=True):\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Convert all NWB files to the standardized format.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n\\n    nwb_files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(data_dir, 'sub-*/sub-*_ses-*.nwb')))\\n    print(f\\\"Found {len(nwb_files)} NWB files\\\")\\n\\n    if max_sessions is not None:\\n        nwb_files = nwb_files[:max_sessions]\\n        print(f\\\"Processing first {max_sessions} files\\\")\\n\\n    # Process all sessions\\n    all_sessions = []\\n    all_subjects = OrderedDict()  # subject_desc -> subject_id\\n    all_regions = OrderedDict()   # region_name -> index\\n\\n    for i, nwb_file in enumerate(nwb_files):\\n        print(f\\\"[{i+1}/{len(nwb_files)}] Processing {os.path.basename(nwb_file)}...\\\")\\n        try:\\n            result = process_session(nwb_file, verbose=verbose)\\n        except Exception as e:\\n            print(f\\\"  ERROR: {e}\\\")\\n            import traceback\\n            traceback.print_exc()\\n            continue\\n\\n        if result is not None:\\n            all_sessions.append(result)\\n            sub_desc = result['subject_desc']\\n            if sub_desc not in all_subjects:\\n                all_subjects[sub_desc] = result['subject_id']\\n            for region in result['unit_regions']:\\n                if region not in all_regions:\\n                    all_regions[region] = len(all_regions)\\n\\n    print(f\\\"\\\\nProcessed {len(all_sessions)} valid sessions from {len(all_subjects)} subjects\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Brain regions ({len(all_regions)}): {list(all_regions.keys())}\\\")\\n\\n    # Build the output data structure\\n    subjects = list(all_subjects.keys())\\n    brain_regions = list(all_regions.keys())\\n\\n    neural = []\\n    inputs = []\\n    outputs = []\\n    subject_idx = []\\n    brain_region_idx = []\\n\\n    total_units = 0\\n    total_trials = 0\\n\\n    for sess in all_sessions:\\n        neural.append(sess['neural'])\\n        inputs.append(sess['input'])\\n        outputs.append(sess['output'])\\n        subject_idx.append(subjects.index(sess['subject_desc']))\\n\\n        # Map unit regions to indices\\n        region_indices = np.array([all_regions[r] for r in sess['unit_regions']], dtype=np.int64)\\n        brain_region_idx.append(region_indices)\\n\\n        total_units += sess['n_good']\\n        total_trials += sess['n_trials']\\n\\n    subject_idx = np.array(subject_idx, dtype=np.int64)\\n\\n    # Define input and output names\\n    input_names = ['time_from_tone_onset', 'photostimulation']\\n    output_names = ['choice', 'outcome', 'early_lick', 'tongue_y_position']\\n    output_values = [\\n        ['left', 'right'],  # choice: 0=left, 1=right\\n        ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit'],  # outcome: 0=ignore, 1=miss, 2=hit\\n        ['no', 'yes'],  # early_lick: 0=no, 1=yes\\n        ['low', 'mid', 'high'],  # tongue_y: 0=<40th, 1=40-60th, 2=>60th\\n    ]\\n\\n    data = {\\n        'neural': neural,\\n        'input': inputs,\\n        'output': outputs,\\n        'subjects': subjects,\\n        'subject_idx': subject_idx,\\n        'brain_regions': brain_regions,\\n        'brain_region_idx': brain_region_idx,\\n        'input_names': input_names,\\n        'output_names': output_names,\\n        'output_values': output_values,\\n        'metadata': {\\n            'task_description': 'Auditory delayed response task: mice report tone frequency (3 or 12 kHz) by licking left or right after a delay period.',\\n            'time_bin_size': BIN_WIDTH * 1000,  # in ms\\n            'temporal_alignment_event': 'Go cue onset',\\n            'off_start': BEGIN_TIME,\\n            'off_end': END_TIME,\\n            'tone_onset_relative_to_go': TONE_ONSET_REL,\\n            'sample_period': 0.65,\\n            'delay_period': 1.2,\\n            'n_sessions': len(all_sessions),\\n            'n_subjects': len(subjects),\\n            'n_brain_regions': len(brain_regions),\\n            'total_units': total_units,\\n            'total_trials': total_trials,\\n            'session_filtering': f'Performance > {MIN_PERFORMANCE:.0%}, >= {MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE} correct trials per lick direction on control trials',\\n            'unit_filtering': \\\"classification == 'good' and non-empty CCF annotation\\\",\\n            'trial_filtering': 'Excluded auto_water and free_water trials. Kept early lick and no-response trials (decoder outputs).',\\n        },\\n    }\\n\\n    # Print summary statistics\\n    print(f\\\"\\\\n=== Data Summary ===\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Sessions: {len(all_sessions)}\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Subjects: {len(subjects)}: {subjects}\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Total units: {total_units}\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Total trials: {total_trials}\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Brain regions: {brain_regions}\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Time bins: {N_BINS} ({BIN_WIDTH*1000:.0f} ms bins)\\\")\\n    print(f\\\"Time window: [{BEGIN_TIME}, {END_TIME}] s relative to go cue\\\")\\n\\n    # Region counts\\n    region_counts = {r: 0 for r in brain_regions}\\n    for sess_br in brain_region_idx:\\n        for idx in sess_br:\\n            region_counts[brain_regions[idx]] += 1\\n    print(f\\\"\\\\nUnits per region:\\\")\\n    for r, c in sorted(region_counts.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):\\n        print(f\\\"  {r}: {c}\\\")\\n\\n    # Save full data\\n    print(f\\\"\\\\nSaving full data to {output_file}...\\\")\\n    with open(output_file, 'wb') as f:\\n        pickle.dump(data, f)\\n    print(f\\\"Saved ({os.path.getsize(output_file) / 1e6:.1f} MB)\\\")\\n\\n    # Save sample data (first 5 sessions)\\n    n_sample = min(5, len(all_sessions))\\n    sample_data = {\\n        'neural': neural[:n_sample],\\n        'input': inputs[:n_sample],\\n        'output': outputs[:n_sample],\\n        'subjects': subjects,\\n        'subject_idx': subject_idx[:n_sample],\\n        'brain_regions': brain_regions,\\n        'brain_region_idx': brain_region_idx[:n_sample],\\n        'input_names': input_names,\\n        'output_names': output_names,\\n        'output_values': output_values,\\n        'metadata': data['metadata'].copy(),\\n    }\\n    sample_data['metadata']['n_sessions'] = n_sample\\n    sample_data['metadata']['note'] = f'Sample of first {n_sample} sessions'\\n\\n    print(f\\\"Saving sample data to {sample_output_file}...\\\")\\n    with open(sample_output_file, 'wb') as f:\\n        pickle.dump(sample_data, f)\\n    print(f\\\"Saved \\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\nConvert NWB data from the MAP dataset to the standardized decoder format.\\\\n\\\\nReference: \\\\\\\"Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding structured across and within brain areas\\\\\\\"\\\\nData: \\\\\\\"Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nProcessing:\\\\n- Temporal alignment: Go cue onset\\\\n- Time window: bins\\\\nBEGIN_TIME = -2.5  # seconds relative to go cue\\\\nEND_TIME = 1.5    # seconds relative to go cue\\\\nTONE_ONSET_REL = -1.85  # tone onset relative to go cue (sample 0.65s + delay 2\\\\n\\\\n# --- Brain region mapping ---\\\\n# Map CCF annotation names to the 14 broad regions used in the paper\\\\n# Based on Allen Brain Atlas CCF ontology and paper methodology\\\\n\\\\ndef map_anno_to_region(anno_name):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Map a CCF annotation name to one of 14 broad brain regions.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    if not anno_name or anno_name.strip() == '':\\\\n        return None\\\\n\\\\n    a = anno_name.strip()\\\\n    al = a.lower()\\\\n\\\\n    # ALM: Secondary motor area (= Anterior Lateral Motor cortex)\\\\n    if 'secondary motor area' in al:\\\\n        return 'ALM'\\\\n\\\\n    # Orbital: Orbital areas and Frontal pole\\\\n    if 'orbital area' in al or 'frontal pole' in al:\\\\n        return 'Orbital'\\\\n\\\\n    # Striatum\\\\n    if al in ('caudoputamen', 'striatum', 'fundus of striatum', 'nucleus accumbens'):\\\\n        return 'Striatum'\\\\n\\\\n    # Pallidum (including septal nuclei, bed nuclei, substantia innominata per Allen CCF)\\\\n    if ('globus pallidus' in al or al == 'pallidum' or\\\\n        'septal nucleus' in al or 'septofimbrial' in al or\\\\n        'triangular nucleus of septum' in al or\\\\n        'substantia innominata' in al or\\\\n        'bed nuclei of the stria terminalis' in al):\\\\n        return 'Pallidum'\\\\n\\\\n    # Hypothalamus (including zona incerta, subthalamic, fields of forel)\\\\n    if ('hypothalamus' in al or 'hypothalamic' in al or\\\\n        'zona incerta' in al or 'fields of forel' in al or\\\\n        'subthalamic' in al or 'lateral preoptic' in al or\\\\n        'tuberomammillary' in al or 'parasubthalamic' in al or\\\\n        'posterior hypothalamic' in al or 'lateral hypothalamic' in al):\\\\n        return 'Hypothalamus'\\\\n\\\\n    # Thalamus (check AFTER hypothalamus to avoid matching \\\\\\\"hypothalamus\\\\\\\")\\\\n    if ('thalamus' in al or 'habenula' in al or\\\\n        'lateral geniculate' in al or 'medial geniculate' in al or\\\\n        'suprageniculate' in al):\\\\n        return 'Thalamus'\\\\n\\\\n    # Cerebellum\\\\n    if ('cerebellum' in al or 'lobule' in al or 'lobules' in al or\\\\n        'simple lobule' in al or 'copula' in al or 'nodulus' in al or\\\\n        'uvula' in al or 'pyramus' in al or 'declive' in al or\\\\n        'paramedian lobule' in al or 'crus ' in al or 'lingula' in al or\\\\n        'fastigial' in al or 'interposed nucleus' in al or\\\\n        'infracerebellar' in al or 'dentate nucleus' in al):\\\\n        return 'Cerebellum'\\\\n\\\\n    # Midbrain\\\\n    if ('midbrain' in al or 'superior colliculus' in al or\\\\n        'inferior colliculus' in al or 'substantia nigra' in al or\\\\n        'red nucleus' in al or 'ventral tegmental' in al or\\\\n        'pretectal' in al or 'pedunculopontine' in al or\\\\n        'periaqueductal' in al or 'peripeduncular' in al or\\\\n        'nucleus of the optic tract' in al or 'nucleus sagulum' in al or\\\\n        'subparafascicular colliculus' in al):\\\\n        return 'Pons'\\\\n\\\\n    # Medulla\\\\n    if ('medulla' in al or 'medullary' in al or\\\\n        'gigantocellular' in al or 'magnocellular' in al or\\\\n        'parvicellular' in al or 'paragigantocellular' in al or\\\\n        'intermediate reticular' in al or 'inferior olivary' in al or\\\\n        'solitary tract' in al or 'vagus' in al or\\\\n        'vestibular' in al or 'facial motor' in al or\\\\n        'trigeminal' in al or 'hypoglossal' in al or\\\\n        'external cuneate' in al or 'lateral reticular nucleus' in al or\\\\n        'parasolitary' in al or 'parapyramidal' in al or\\\\n        'nucleus raphe' in al or 'nucleus of roller' in al or\\\\n        'nucleus x' in al):\\\\n        return 'Medulla'\\\\n\\\\n    # Hippocampus\\\\n    if ('field ca' in al or 'dentate gyrus' in al or\\\\n        'subiculum' in al or 'postsubiculum' in al or\\\\n        'hippocampal' in al or 'entorhinal' in al):\\\\n        return 'Hippocampus'\\\\n\\\\n    # Olfactory\\\\n    if ('olfactory' in al or 'piriform' in al or 'taenia tecta' in al):\\\\n        return 'Olfactory'\\\\n\\\\n    # Cortical subplate (amygdala, claustrum, endopiriform)\\\\n    if ('amygdal' in al or 'claustrum' in al or 'endopiriform' in al or\\\\n        'cortical subplate' in al or 'intercalated' in al):\\\\n        return 'CorticalSubplate'\\\\n\\\\n    # OtherCortex: remaining cortical areas\\\\n    cortex_keywords = [\\\\n        'primary motor', 'primary somatosensory', 'primary visual',\\\\n        'primary auditory', 'supplemental somatosensory',\\\\n        'gustatory', 'visceral area', 'retrosplenial',\\\\n        'temporal association', 'ectorhinal', 'perirhinal',\\\\n        'anterior cingulate',    'area, layer', 'area, layer',  # catch remaining cortical layers\\\\n    ]\\\\n    for kw in cortex_keywords:\\\\n        if kw in al:\\\\n            return 'OtherCortex'\\\\n\\\\n    # If contains \\\\\\\"layer\\\\\\\" it's likely cortex\\\\n    if 'layer' in al:\\\\n        return 'OtherCortex'\\\\n\\\\n    # Fallback: print warning and return None\\\\n    print(f\\\\\\\"  WARNING: Unmapped annotation: '{anno_name}'\\\\\\\")\\\\n    return None\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef compute_firing_rates(spike_times, go_cue_time, begin_time, end_time, bin_edges):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    Compute firing rates for a single unit across trials.\\\\n\\\\n    Args:\\\\n        spike_times: array of spike times (absolute session time)\\\\n        go_cue_time: absolute time of go cue for this trial\\\\n        begin_time, end_time: time window relative to go cue\\\\n        bin_edges: array of bin edges relative to go cue\\\\n\\\\n    Returns:\\\\n        firing_rates: array of shape (n_bins,) - firing rates in Hz\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    # Convert to relative time\\\\n    rel_spikes = spike_times - go_cue_time\\\\n    # Keep only spikes within window\\\\n    mask = (rel_spikes >= begin_time) & (rel_spikes < end_time)\\\\n    rel_spikes = rel_spikes[mask]\\\\n    # Bin spikes\\\\n    counts, _ = np.histogram(rel_spikes, bins=bin_edges)\\\\n    # Convert to firing rate (Hz)\\\\n    firing_rates = counts / BIN_WIDTH\\\\n    return firing_rates\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef process_session(nwb_file, verbose=True):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    Process a single NWB file (session) and return formatted data.\\\\n\\\\n    Returns:\\\\n        session_data dict or None if session doesn't meet criteria\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    io = ({len(go_start_times)}) != n_trials ({n_trials_total})\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n    # --- Filter trials: exclude auto_water and free_water ---\\\\n    valid_trial_mask = (trials['auto_water'].values == 0) & (trials['free_water'].values == 0)\\\\n\\\\n    # --- Session filtering: compute performance on CONTROL trials ---\\\\n    # Control trials = no photostim, no auto_water, no free_water, no early lick\\\\n    control_mask = (valid_trial_mask &\\\\n                    (trials['early_lick'].values == 'no early') &\\\\n                    (trials['outcome'].values != 'ignore'))\\\\n\\\\n    # Check photostim: N/A means no photostim\\\\n    photostim_power = trials['photostim_power'].values\\\\n    no_photostim = np.array([str(p) == 'N/A' or str(p) == 'nan' or (isinstance(p, (int, float)) fraction correct among control trials\\\\n    n_correct = (control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit').sum()\\\\n    performance = n_correct / n_control\\\\n\\\\n    # Count correct left and right\\\\n    correct_left = ((control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit') &\\\\n                    (control_trials['trial_instruction'].values == 'left')).sum()\\\\n    correct_right = ((control_trials['outcome'].values == 'hit') &\\\\n                     (control_trials['trial_instruction'].values == 'right')).sum()\\\\n\\\\n    if performance < MIN_PERFORMANCE:\\\\n        if verbose:\\\\n            print(f\\\\\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: performance {performance:.2%} < {MIN_PERFORMANCE:.0%}\\\\\\\")\\\\n        io.close()\\\\n        return None\\\\n\\\\n    if correct_left < MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE or correct_right < MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE:\\\\n        if verbose:\\\\n            print(f\\\\\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: correct L={correct_left}, R={correct_right} (need {MIN_CORRECT_PER_SIDE})\\\\\\\")\\\\n        io.close()\\\\n        return None\\\\n\\\\n    # --- Get valid trial indices ---\\\\n    valid_indices = np.where(valid_trial_mask)[0]\\\\n    n_trials = len(valid_indices)\\\\n\\\\n    if n_trials < 2:\\\\n        if verbose:\\\\n            print(f\\\\\\\"  SKIP {sess_name}: only {n_trials} valid trials\\\\\\\")\\\\n        io.close()\\\\n        return None\\\\n\\\\n    # --- Get unit info ---\\\\n    units = nwb.units\\\\n    n_units_total = len(units)\\\\n    classification = units['classification'].data[:]\\\\n    anno_names = units['anno_name'].data[:]\\\\n\\\\n    # Filter to good units with valid annotations\\\\n    good_mask = classification == 'good'\\\\n    good_indices = np.where(good_mask)[0]\\\\n\\\\n    # Map annotations to regions and filter out unmapped units\\\\n    unit_regions = []\\\\n    final_unit_indices = []\\\\n    for ui in good_indices:\\\\n        region = map_anno_to_region(anno_names[ui])\\\\n        if region is not None:\\\\n            unit_regions.append(region)\\\\n            final_unit_indices.append(ui)\\\\n\\\\n    n_good =
